title: Inferencing for Enterprises
gist: JPMorganChase AI-infrastructure product lead Dio Rettori argues enterprise inference is six problems at once — hard, expensive, ever-changing, and a data-sovereignty, dependency and regulatory problem — citing ~$16–20M three-year TCO for 64 B200s (on-prem ≈ AWS reserved), 41% vs 5.2% latency variance cloud vs self-controlled, and a case that RAG has a ceiling so business ontology should be baked into models via RL/fine-tuning. Views are personal, not JPMorgan's.

insights.claim: Dio Rettori argues inference is deep systems engineering distinct from training: training resembles HPC (priority queues, topology-aware GPU clusters), while inference is real-time, latency-sensitive, stateful and bursty, and the skill sets do not necessarily overlap.
insights.speaker: Dio Rettori
insights.so_what: Inference-serving talent and tooling are a separate market from training infra.
insights.locator: Training vs. Inference

insights.claim: The industry is specialising hardware for inference, with NVIDIA partnering with an inference-focused chipset company (Grok, per the speaker) and Cerebras pursuing very large silicon dies surrounded by more memory, at the cost of larger blast radius when a die fails.
insights.speaker: Dio Rettori
insights.so_what: Inference-specific silicon is a growing segment; watch NVIDIA's inference partnerships and wafer-scale players.
insights.locator: Now the industry is going in a specialization route

insights.claim: Tokenization in an LLM inference call runs on the CPU, not the GPU, so inference needs both, and any point where the GPU starves for data wastes money.
insights.speaker: Dio Rettori
insights.so_what: CPU demand rides alongside GPU demand in inference fleets.
insights.locator: Inside an inferencing call

insights.claim: KV cache grows with context length and spilling to CPU memory during inference severely slows processing, making memory-saving techniques like quantization (e.g., the TurboQuant paper) critical, though lossless results are hard to guarantee.
insights.speaker: Dio Rettori
insights.so_what: HBM capacity and memory-efficiency techniques are binding constraints on inference economics.
insights.locator: Inference is a Hard Technical Problem

insights.claim: Agents multiply inference load, making batching and scheduling — matching synchronous versus overnight batchable work to infrastructure — a core utilization lever.
insights.speaker: Dio Rettori
insights.so_what: Agentic adoption is a multiplier on inference compute demand.
insights.quote: Agents make this all go crazy because it's just multiplying everything.
insights.locator: Within inferencing, it's just called batching

insights.claim: A Cast AI report cited by Rettori found only 5% GPU utilization across the systems it studied, along with CPU over-provisioning.
insights.speaker: Dio Rettori
insights.so_what: Massive GPU underutilization implies efficiency tooling upside — and a risk that some GPU demand is wasteful.
insights.locator: Inference is an Expensive Problem

insights.claim: GPUs fail far more often than other hardware — a vendor told Rettori around 10% failure, and companies are reportedly comfortable at ~5% — due to sensitivity to temperature and radiation, including solar flares, so fleets must be over-bought.
insights.speaker: Dio Rettori
insights.so_what: GPU failure rates inflate effective unit demand and spare-parts needs, supportive of GPU volume.
insights.locator: Again, cost is real

insights.claim: Rettori estimates a three-year total cost of ownership of $16–20 million for a 64-GPU NVIDIA B200 system, including hardware, software licenses, spares, services, power and cooling, but excluding inference software, operating team and model licensing.
insights.speaker: Dio Rettori
insights.so_what: Benchmark for enterprise on-prem AI capex: ~$250–300K per B200 over three years all-in.
insights.locator: A quick game for us here

insights.claim: Renting 64 B200s on AWS P6-B200 capacity blocks with a three-year reservation costs roughly the same as owning them on-prem, but owned GPUs that outlast three years and are amortized become a win thereafter.
insights.speaker: Dio Rettori
insights.so_what: Cloud vs on-prem GPU price parity at 3-year commitments; GPU useful life beyond 3 years is a key variable for both enterprises and hyperscaler depreciation debates.
insights.locator: Capacity blocks already assume

insights.claim: Rettori argues sound enterprises should use on-prem, cloud and pay-per-token APIs together, because single-vendor dependence for inference is not a sound business practice.
insights.speaker: Dio Rettori
insights.so_what: Enterprise AI spend will be multi-sourced, limiting any one provider's lock-in.
insights.quote: It's not a sound business practice to have single vendors for mostly anything.
insights.locator: Then there is a big differentiator

insights.claim: Every inference call to an external API is a data transfer decision; contractual no-training clauses do not stop data leaving the enterprise perimeter, so global firms need control of where inference runs.
insights.speaker: Dio Rettori
insights.so_what: Data-residency demands favour self-hosted/regional inference and sovereign-AI offerings.
insights.quote: Every inference call to an external API is a data transfer decision, whether or not you treat it as one.
insights.locator: Inference is a Data Sovereignty Problem

insights.claim: Most enterprises depend on a small set of foundation model providers, concentrating pricing, capacity and capability risk they cannot control, such as unannounced behaviour changes between model versions.
insights.speaker: Dio Rettori
insights.so_what: Concentration risk is a driver for open-weight model adoption and multi-provider routing.
insights.locator: Inference is a Dependency Problem

insights.claim: Inference is becoming a regulatory problem: the EU AI Act requires logging and proof of how decisions were made, and US states including Colorado, New York and California are following similar patterns, so global firms will comply with the most restrictive regime.
insights.speaker: Dio Rettori
insights.so_what: AI governance, logging and audit tooling has regulatory demand tailwinds even without US federal rules.
insights.locator: Inference is a Regulatory Problem

insights.claim: Every SaaS vendor an enterprise contracts uses many further third parties, so without strong vendor oversight a company loses control of where its data goes.
insights.speaker: Dio Rettori
insights.so_what: Third-party risk management is a gating factor for enterprise AI SaaS sales.
insights.locator: There you have customer assets information

insights.claim: Rettori believes most agentic workloads will be system-to-system rather than human-replacing, and these are far more sensitive to latency variance — e.g., a payment workflow cannot take an unpredictable 1 to 35 seconds.
insights.speaker: Dio Rettori
insights.so_what: Transactional agent use cases will demand latency SLAs, a premium product for inference providers.
insights.locator: A lot of the workloads that we see

insights.claim: In Rettori's demo of a six-agent sequential workflow, latency variation was 41% via a cloud API versus 5.2% running on his own controlled hardware, though he admits tuning the local run.
insights.speaker: Dio Rettori
insights.so_what: Controlled infrastructure buys determinism; providers selling deterministic response times at a premium have a market.
insights.quote: The variation for when doing the call on cloud was 41%. The variation when running on-prem was 5.2%.
insights.locator: Determinism is hard

insights.claim: Most inference providers sell more deterministic response times at extra cost, so control of latency can be obtained contractually, not only by owning hardware.
insights.speaker: Dio Rettori
insights.so_what: Latency guarantees are a monetizable tier for inference API vendors.
insights.locator: I hacked it a little bit

themes.theme: RAG ceiling and ontology in models

insights.claim: Rettori contends RAG is statistical rather than truly semantic search and, citing a Google paper, has a mathematical ceiling: beyond ~50,000 similar documents, fixed-size embedding vectors cannot represent the differences.
insights.speaker: Dio Rettori
insights.so_what: Limits of vector retrieval challenge the RAG/vector-DB growth narrative for large similar corpora.
insights.locator: I can just never-ending forever RAG

insights.claim: Rettori predicts reinforcement learning pipelines will explode as enterprises try to bake business and process ontology directly into the models they control, reducing agent calls, RAG and processing time.
insights.speaker: Dio Rettori
insights.so_what: Demand shift toward fine-tuning/RL infrastructure and open, trainable models.
insights.locator: Retrieval does not understand a lot

insights.claim: Enterprises cannot fine-tune a model they do not control, so Rettori recommends investing in trainable (open) models and self-hosting with real understanding and ownership of the stack.
insights.speaker: Dio Rettori
insights.so_what: Supports open-weight model ecosystems and enterprise GPU ownership.
insights.locator: Retrieval does not understand a lot

insights.claim: Agents lack the codes of conduct and self-preservation incentives that make humans apply guardrails, so every human policy must be codified for agents; Rettori suggests counting agentic-governance job postings as an adoption gauge.
insights.speaker: Dio Rettori
insights.so_what: Agentic governance roles and tooling are an emerging category to watch.
insights.locator: I think it's starting
